issues.legal_issue: For income from a building, the person entitled to receive that income in their own right may be treated as the owner for tax under the house-property head even without a registered conveyance.
material_facts: The assessee-company had paid the consideration for four flats, taken possession, let them to tenants, and received rental income, although title had not been conveyed to it through a registered document.
An individual assessee had paid the full price for three flats, taken possession, exercised control over them, let them to tenants, and received rent, although no sale deeds had been executed.
In another appeal, the tribunal found that the assessee owned the flats and parking space from which rental income was received.
issues.conclusion: The income was assessable as income from house property under Section 22, not as income from other sources under Section 56. The absence of a registered conveyance did not by itself prevent a person entitled to the property’s income in their own right from being treated as its owner for this purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 22 and 56 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, distinguish income chargeable as income from house property from income chargeable as income from other sources. Applying R.B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala v. Commissioner of Income Tax, the Court held that, for Section 22, the owner is the person who can exercise the rights of ownership in their own right and is entitled to the property income in their own right; legal title alone is not decisive. The Court considered the practical rights of possession, control and enjoyment, including the protection afforded to a transferee in possession under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. It also relied on the principle of updating construction discussed in State v. S.J. Chaudhary.

predicates.income_head_classification_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the tax classification of income derived from a building.
predicates.income_from_building: The assessee derived income from a building or property consisting of a building.
predicates.entitled_to_property_income_in_own_right: The assessee was entitled to receive and use the property's income in their own right, rather than receiving it for another person.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns the tax classification of building income and the assessee is entitled to that income in their own right, the income is assessed as income from house property.

issues.legal_issue: The amendment defining persons treated as owners for house-property taxation was clarificatory and applied retrospectively.
material_facts: At the time the relevant income was assessed, the High Courts had taken conflicting views on whether a person in possession under a sale arrangement, but without a registered conveyance, could be treated as an owner.

The amendment expanded the categories of persons treated as owners, and its explanatory materials described the change as addressing uncertainty and practical problems concerning ownership and taxation of property income.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was declaratory and clarificatory in nature and applied retrospectively insofar as it concerned the specified deemed-owner categories.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles governing declaratory and clarificatory legislation, including those discussed in Crawford's Statutory Construction, Francis Bennion's Statutory Interpretation and G.P. Singh's Principles of Statutory Interpretation. It relied on Keshavlal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas for the principle that an explanatory enactment may supply an omission or clear up doubt about the meaning of existing law. It concluded that the amendment to Section 27(iii), (iiia) and (iiib) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, clarified the meaning of ownership for Section 22 and therefore operated retrospectively.

predicates.tax_amendment_interpretation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a tax-law amendment applies to periods before its enactment.
predicates.amendment_addresses_uncertainty_in_exist: The amendment was introduced against conflicting interpretations or uncertainty about an existing legal definition.
predicates.amendment_clarifies_existing_rule: The amendment's purpose and effect are to explain or clarify the existing rule rather than to introduce a new rule.

issues.definition: If a tax amendment addresses uncertainty in an existing definition and clarifies the existing rule, it applies to prior periods.
